questions.stem: Which of these numbers is irrational?
questions.explanation: 20 is not a perfect square, so √20 has a decimal expansion (about 4.4721…) that never terminates and never repeats, which makes it irrational. The most tempting wrong choice is √36: it looks like a surd, but 36 is a perfect square so √36 is exactly 6, a whole number. The cue is to check whether the number under the root sign is a perfect square (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, …) before deciding.
questions.teaching:
Numbers divide into two families depending on whether they can be written as one whole number over another.

Those that can are rational, and the family is larger than people expect: all whole numbers, all terminating decimals, and all recurring decimals qualify. Those that cannot are irrational, and their decimals run forever without settling into a repeating pattern — π is the famous case, and so is the square root of any whole number that is not a perfect square. So checking a root means asking whether it simplifies exactly.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes an irrational number?
options: It is any decimal that has more than about ten decimal places when written out
It is any number that cannot be written as a decimal at all, only as a surd
Its decimal expansion goes on forever without ever settling into a repeating pattern
Its decimal expansion goes on forever and eventually repeats a block of digits
questions.explanation: A number is rational exactly when its decimal either terminates or repeats a block forever; an irrational number therefore has a non-terminating, non-repeating expansion. The option about a repeating block describes rational numbers such as 1/3 = 0.333… or 5/11 = 0.4545…, so it is the reverse of the truth. Look for a pattern that repeats: if you can find one, the number is rational.

questions.stem: A square garden bed has an area of 20 m². What can be said about the length of one side?
options: It is √20 m, an irrational length of about 4.47 m
It is √20 m, which is rational because 20 is a whole number
It is exactly 4.5 m, since 4.5 × 4.5 gives an area of 20 m²
It is 5 m, because the side of a square is always the area divided by 4
questions.explanation: Side length is the square root of the area, and 20 is not a perfect square, so √20 = 4.4721… is irrational; 4.47 m is only a rounded value. The claim that √20 is rational because 20 is a whole number confuses the number under the root with the root itself — 20 is rational, but its square root is not. Also note 4.5 × 4.5 = 20.25, not 20, so 4.5 is not exact.

questions.stem: A student says 'if you multiply two irrational numbers you must get another irrational number'. Which response shows this is wrong?
options: √8 × √2 = √16 = 4, so two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational number
√8 × √2 = √10, and √10 is rational because 10 is not a perfect square
π × π = π², and π² is rational because squaring removes the irrational part
√2 × √3 = √6, which is rational because 2 and 3 are both rational numbers
questions.explanation: √8 and √2 are both irrational, yet their product is √16, which equals exactly 4 — a counterexample that disproves the claim. The suggestion that √2 × √3 = √6 is rational is tempting because 2 and 3 are rational, but 6 is not a perfect square, so √6 = 2.449… is irrational. When multiplying surds, work out the number under the root first and check whether it is a perfect square.

questions.stem: Which of these expressions has a rational value?
questions.explanation: Both 9 and 16 are perfect squares, so √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7, a whole number and therefore rational. The trickiest distractor is √5 × √3, which equals √15; since 15 is not a perfect square, this is irrational, even though the two surds have been combined neatly. Dividing or multiplying π by a rational number also leaves it irrational, so π ÷ 2 is irrational.

questions.stem: A square floor tile has sides of 5 cm, so its diagonal measures √50 cm. What can be said about this diagonal length?
options: It is irrational, because 50 is not a perfect square, so √50 has a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal
It is rational, because the side length 5 is a whole number and the diagonal comes from whole numbers
It is rational, because √50 can be rewritten as 5√2, and 5√2 is a fraction of two exact values
It is irrational, because the diagonal of any shape can never be given as an exact rational measurement
questions.explanation: The square root of a positive whole number is rational only when that number is a perfect square; 50 sits between 49 and 64, so √50 cannot be written as an integer divided by a natural number and is irrational. The tempting option is the one saying it is rational because 5 is a whole number — but squaring and square-rooting whole numbers does not preserve rationality of the root, since √50 ≈ 7.0710678... never terminates or repeats. Rewriting as 5√2 does not help either, because √2 is itself irrational. Cue: check whether the number under the root sign is a perfect square.

questions.stem: What is 3^4 × 3^5 written as a single power?
questions.explanation: When multiplying powers with the same base, the base stays the same and the exponents are added: 4 + 5 = 9, so the answer is 3^9. The tempting wrong answer is 3^20, which comes from multiplying the exponents instead of adding them — multiplying exponents belongs to the 'power of a power' law, not to multiplying two powers. The cue is the multiplication sign between two separate powers: same base, add the exponents.
questions.teaching:
Multiplying powers of the same base combines them into a single power, and the reason is worth seeing rather than memorising.

Each power is a row of that base multiplied together. Multiplying two of them just puts all the copies in one row, so you count how many there are altogether — which tells you what happens to the two indices. The rule only works when the bases match. Multiplying the indices instead of adding them is the classic error; that rule belongs to raising a power to another power.

questions.stem: Simplify 7^8 ÷ 7^2 as a single power.
questions.explanation: Dividing powers with the same base means subtracting the exponents: 8 - 2 = 6, giving 7^6. Wait for the trap 7^4, which comes from dividing the exponents (8 ÷ 2) — division applies to the powers, not to the exponents themselves. Remember: division of powers matches subtraction of exponents, just as multiplication of powers matches addition.
questions.teaching:
Dividing powers of the same base is easier if you picture writing them out in full.

The top is a row of that base multiplied together, and so is the bottom. Cancelling pairs leaves however many are left over on top — which tells you what happens to the indices. So division subtracts them, just as multiplication adds them. Both rules require the same base; you cannot combine powers of different bases this way. Dividing the indices instead of subtracting is the standard error.

questions.stem: What is the value of 5^0?
questions.explanation: Any non-zero number raised to the power of zero equals 1, because 5^3 ÷ 5^3 = 5^0 and any number divided by itself is 1. The most common error is answering 0, from thinking the exponent 0 makes the whole expression zero — but the exponent counts how many factors are used, and using none leaves the multiplicative identity, 1. Cue: a zero exponent always gives 1 (for a non-zero base), never 0.
questions.teaching:
Any non-zero number raised to the power of zero gives the same result, and the pattern shows why.

Descending through the powers of any base, each step divides by that base: 5³ is 125, 5² is 25, 5¹ is 5. Take one more step down and you divide once more, which pins the value exactly. It also follows from the division rule: any number divided by itself equals one, and subtracting equal indices leaves zero. Answering zero comes from reading the index as the result, which is the trap here.

questions.stem: Which of these is equal to 2^10?
questions.explanation: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, and 6 + 4 = 10, so 2^6 × 2^4 = 2^10. The trap is (2^5)^5, where students see two 5s and think 5 + 5 = 10, but a power of a power multiplies the exponents, giving 2^25. Check which operation is being done first: multiply powers → add exponents; raise a power to a power → multiply exponents.

questions.stem: Write (2^3)^4 as a single power of 2.
questions.explanation: Raising a power to another power multiplies the exponents: 3 × 4 = 12, so the result is 2^12. The answer 2^7 comes from adding the exponents, which is the rule for multiplying two separate powers of the same base, not for a bracketed power. Look for the bracket: brackets with an outside exponent mean multiply the exponents.

questions.stem: Find the value of (6^5 × 6^3) ÷ 6^6.
questions.explanation: Add the exponents for the multiplication (5 + 3 = 8), then subtract for the division (8 - 6 = 2), giving 6^2 = 36. The answer 1296 is 6^4, which comes from subtracting incorrectly or from only using one of the two exponents on top. Always combine the numerator into a single power first, then subtract the denominator's exponent.

questions.stem: Which reasoning correctly establishes that 7^0 = 1?
options: 7^0 is the same as 7 × 0, and multiplying by zero always gives 0
Powers always begin counting at the base itself, so 7^0 = 7
7^3 ÷ 7^3 = 7^(3-3) = 7^0, and any number divided by itself is 1
7^0 means no sevens are multiplied at all, so the total must be 0
questions.explanation: The zero exponent comes from the division law: dividing a power by itself gives an exponent of 0, and the same division obviously equals 1, so 7^0 must be 1. The most tempting alternative says 7^0 means no sevens are multiplied so the answer is 0, but multiplying no factors leaves the multiplicative identity 1, not 0. The reliable cue is to test the rule with a division such as 7^3 ÷ 7^3.

questions.stem: Write 9^4 × 3^2 as a single power of 3.
questions.explanation: First rewrite the bases the same way: 9 = 3^2, so 9^4 = (3^2)^4 = 3^8, and then 3^8 × 3^2 = 3^10. The answer 3^8 is tempting because students convert 9^4 correctly but forget to add the extra exponent 2 from the second factor. The exponent laws only apply once every power has the same base, so always convert first, then combine.

questions.stem: Written as a decimal, the fraction 3/8 is:
questions.explanation: A fraction means numerator divided by denominator, so 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, which terminates because 8 is made only of factors of 2. The tempting choice 0.38 comes from rounding 0.375 to two decimal places, but the exact value is asked for, and 3/8 stops neatly after three decimal places. Checking 2.666... shows the division was done the wrong way round (8 ÷ 3), so always divide the top number by the bottom number.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about converting any fraction with whole-number numerator and non-zero whole-number denominator into a decimal?
options: The decimal will either terminate or recur
The decimal will always terminate after a few places
The decimal will always recur with a repeating block
The decimal may go on forever with no repeating pattern
questions.explanation: Dividing whole numbers can only produce a finite set of possible remainders, so the division either finishes exactly (terminating) or a remainder repeats and the digits cycle (recurring). Saying it will always terminate ignores fractions such as 1/3 = 0.333..., and saying it always recurs ignores 1/4 = 0.25. A decimal that never terminates and never repeats belongs to irrational numbers such as π, which cannot be written as a fraction of whole numbers.

questions.stem: Write 0.45 as a fraction in simplest form.
questions.explanation: Two decimal places means hundredths, so 0.45 = 45/100, and dividing top and bottom by 5 gives 9/20. Choosing 9/25 comes from dividing 45 by 5 but 100 by 4, which is not the same divisor top and bottom. Always simplify by dividing both numbers by the same common factor, and check by dividing back: 9 ÷ 20 = 0.45.
questions.teaching:
Converting a decimal to a fraction starts from what the decimal places actually mean.

The first place is tenths, the second hundredths, the third thousandths. So a two-place decimal is that many hundredths, which gives you the fraction immediately — then simplify by dividing top and bottom by their highest common factor. The simplification step is where marks are lost, since an unsimplified answer is usually not accepted. Check by dividing your fraction back out and confirming you get the original decimal.

questions.stem: Which of these fractions converts to a terminating decimal?
questions.explanation: A fraction in simplest form terminates exactly when its denominator has only 2s and 5s as prime factors; 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5, so 9/40 = 0.225. The closest trap is 5/12, because 12 looks like a friendly even number, but 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and that factor of 3 forces recurring digits (0.41666...). Factorise the denominator first: any prime other than 2 or 5 means the decimal recurs.

questions.stem: Using division, 5/11 as a decimal is:
questions.explanation: Dividing 5 by 11 gives remainders that cycle between 5 and 6, producing the repeating block 45 forever, so 5/11 = 0.454545... The option 0.4545 exactly is the calculator display cut short; the true value never stops, since 11 is not made from 2s and 5s. The choice 0.545454... reverses the repeating digits, which you can rule out by estimating: 5/11 is a little less than half.

questions.stem: The recurring decimal 0.8333... (the 3 repeats forever) equals which fraction?
questions.explanation: Only the 3 repeats, and 5 ÷ 6 = 0.8333..., so the fraction is 5/6. The option 83/99 is what you get by wrongly assuming the whole block 83 repeats, since 83/99 = 0.838383... A quick check is to divide each candidate: 8/9 gives 0.888... and 83/100 gives exactly 0.83, so neither matches.

questions.stem: Write the recurring decimal 0.363636... in simplest fraction form.
questions.explanation: A two-digit repeating block over 99 gives 36/99, and dividing top and bottom by 9 gives 4/11, which checks out since 4 ÷ 11 = 0.363636... The option 9/25 comes from treating the number as the terminating decimal 0.36, which is slightly smaller than the recurring value. Remember: one repeating digit sits over 9, two repeating digits sit over 99.

questions.stem: Convert 7/40 into a decimal.
questions.explanation: A fraction means numerator divided by denominator, so 7 ÷ 40 = 0.175 (you can check: 40 × 0.175 = 7). The tempting answer 1.75 comes from dividing 7 by 4 instead of 40, and 0.0175 comes from dividing by 400; 5.714285714... is 40 ÷ 7, the division done the wrong way round. The cue: since 7 is smaller than 40, the decimal must be less than 1, and 40 goes into 7 about 0.17 times, so 0.175 is the only sensible size.

questions.stem: Calculate -7 - (-12).
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding its opposite, so -7 - (-12) becomes -7 + 12 = 5. The tempting answer -19 comes from treating the two negative signs as a single subtraction and working out -7 - 12. The cue is the bracketed negative: two minus signs side by side turn into a plus.
questions.teaching:
Subtracting a negative number is the operation that causes the most trouble, and there is one rule that resolves it.

Two negative signs next to each other cancel, turning the subtraction into an addition. Thinking of it on a number line helps: subtracting means moving left, and subtracting a negative reverses that direction, so you move right instead. Rewriting the expression with the double sign resolved before doing any arithmetic is the safest habit, because it turns an error-prone step into an ordinary one.

questions.stem: What is 2/3 + 1/4?
questions.explanation: Fractions must be rewritten with a common denominator before adding: 2/3 = 8/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so the sum is 11/12. The answer 3/7 comes from adding numerators and denominators separately, which is not how addition of fractions works. Check by size: 2/3 alone is more than a half, so any correct answer must be bigger than 1/2.
questions.teaching:
Fractions can only be added when they are cut into pieces of the same size, so unlike denominators must be made alike first.

Find a common denominator — the lowest common multiple of the two is tidiest — then convert each fraction by multiplying top and bottom by the same amount, which changes how it is written without changing its value. Only then add the numerators, leaving the denominator alone. Adding the denominators together is the classic error, and a quick sanity check catches it: the answer must be larger than either fraction you started with.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate for 3.9 × 48?
questions.explanation: Rounding to easy numbers gives 4 × 50 = 200, which is close to the exact value of 187.2. The estimate 120 comes from rounding both numbers down too far, to 3 and 40, which throws the estimate well below the true answer. Round each factor to the nearest convenient number, not to the smallest convenient one.
questions.teaching:
Estimating means rounding each number to something easy and doing the calculation mentally, to check whether an exact answer is plausible.

Round each figure to one significant figure or to a convenient nearby number, then multiply. The point is not accuracy but scale: the estimate tells you roughly what size the answer should be, so a calculator slip that lands ten times out is obvious immediately. It is worth doing before any long calculation, because catching an error early is far cheaper than finding it at the end.

questions.explanation: Brackets first: 3 - 7 = -4, so -4 × (-4) = 16, and 12 ÷ (-2) = -6, giving 16 - 6 = 10. The answer 22 comes from treating 12 ÷ (-2) as +6 and adding it, ignoring that dividing a positive by a negative gives a negative. Remember a negative times a negative is positive, but a positive divided by a negative is negative.

questions.stem: Calculate 3/4 ÷ 2/5.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8. The answer 3/10 comes from multiplying the two fractions as they stand instead of flipping the second one. Only the fraction you are dividing BY gets turned upside down, and since 2/5 is less than 1 the answer must be larger than 3/4.

questions.stem: Calculate 8.4 ÷ 0.4.
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 10 to make the divisor a whole number: 84 ÷ 4 = 21. The answer 2.1 comes from assuming that dividing always makes a number smaller, but dividing by a number less than 1 gives a larger result. As a check, ask how many lots of 0.4 fit into 8.4 — clearly more than 8.

questions.stem: A diver is 12.5 m below sea level. She rises 4.75 m, then descends 6.25 m. What is her final depth?
questions.explanation: Taking below sea level as negative: -12.5 + 4.75 = -7.75, then -7.75 - 6.25 = -14, so she is 14 m below the surface. The answer 3 m below sea level comes from adding the two moves first (4.75 + 6.25 = 11) and subtracting that from 12.5, which wrongly treats the descent as an upward move. Track the sign of each move separately: rising is positive, descending is negative.

questions.stem: For a multiplication of two positive decimals, which rounding strategy is guaranteed to produce an estimate larger than the exact answer?
options: Round both factors up before multiplying
Round both factors down before multiplying
Round the larger factor up and the smaller factor down
Round each factor to the nearest whole number before multiplying
questions.explanation: With positive numbers, increasing both factors can only increase the product, so rounding both up always overestimates. Rounding the larger factor up and the smaller one down is tempting, but the two changes pull in opposite directions, so the estimate could land above or below the true value. Rounding to the nearest whole number likewise gives no guarantee of direction.

questions.stem: A bicycle priced at $80 is increased in price by 15%. What is the new price?
questions.explanation: A 15% increase means the new price is 115% of the old price, so 80 × 1.15 = 92. The option $95 comes from treating the 15% as $15 and adding it, but 15% of $80 is $12, not $15. Watch for the word 'of': a percentage is always a fraction of the original amount, so convert to a multiplier (1.15) rather than adding the number itself.

questions.stem: Which single calculation decreases an amount by 12%?
questions.explanation: After a 12% decrease, 88% of the amount remains, so the multiplier is 88 ÷ 100 = 0.88. Multiplying by 1.12 is the multiplier for a 12% increase, not a decrease. The quick check is that a decrease multiplier must be less than 1 and an increase multiplier must be greater than 1.

questions.stem: Which calculation gives the percentage error of a measurement?
options: The size of the difference between measured and actual, divided by the actual value, times 100
The size of the difference between measured and actual, divided by the measured value, times 100
The difference between the measured value and the actual value, with no division
The actual value divided by the size of the difference, times 100
questions.explanation: Percentage error compares the size of the error with the true (actual) value, so you divide the difference by the actual value and multiply by 100. Dividing by the measured value is the common slip — the measured value is the one that may be wrong, so it cannot be the benchmark. Remember: the denominator is always the value you are trying to hit.

questions.stem: A student measures a rod as 48 cm, but its actual length is 50 cm. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: The error is 50 - 48 = 2 cm, and percentage error is 2 ÷ 50 × 100 = 4%. Choosing 4.17% comes from dividing by the measured 48 cm instead of the actual 50 cm. Choosing 2% treats the 2 cm difference as if it were already a percentage.

questions.stem: A jacket costs $60. Its price is increased by 20%, and later the new price is decreased by 20%. What is the final price?
questions.explanation: The two changes act on different amounts: 60 × 1.2 = 72, then 72 × 0.8 = 57.60. The answer $60.00 assumes the increase and decrease cancel, but the 20% reduction is taken from the larger price of $72, so more is removed than was added. Whenever percentage changes are applied one after another, multiply the multipliers rather than adding or cancelling the percentages.

questions.stem: In a sale, all prices are reduced by 25%. A pair of shoes has a sale price of $54. What was the price before the sale?
questions.explanation: The sale price is 75% of the original, so the original is 54 ÷ 0.75 = $72. The tempting answer $67.50 comes from adding 25% to $54, but the 25% discount was calculated from the larger original price, not from $54. For reverse percentage problems, divide by the multiplier instead of applying a new percentage to the reduced amount.

questions.stem: A shop raises the marked price of every item by 30%, then advertises '30% off everything'. Compared with the original prices, the advertised prices are:
options: exactly equal to the original prices
questions.explanation: The combined multiplier is 1.3 × 0.7 = 0.91, which is a 9% decrease overall. Thinking the prices are unchanged assumes the +30% and -30% cancel, but the discount is taken from the raised price, so the fall in dollars is larger than the rise. Combining percentage changes always means multiplying multipliers, never adding or subtracting the percentages.

questions.stem: Organisers estimated that 250 people would attend a concert, but only 200 people came. What is the percentage error of the estimate?
questions.explanation: The actual value is 200, and the error is 250 - 200 = 50, so the percentage error is 50 ÷ 200 × 100 = 25%. The answer 20% comes from dividing the error by the estimate of 250, but percentage error is always measured against the true value. Identify which number is the actual figure first, then use it as the denominator.

questions.stem: In a business context, which statement correctly defines profit?
options: Profit is the cost price minus the selling price
Profit is the selling price divided by the cost price
Profit is the selling price added to the cost price
Profit is the selling price minus the cost price
questions.explanation: Profit measures how much more you receive than you paid, so you subtract the cost price from the selling price; if the answer is negative it is a loss. Saying profit is the cost price minus the selling price reverses the subtraction, which actually gives the loss when an item sells for less than it cost. The cue is the order: money in first, money out second.

questions.stem: A market stall buys 50 badges for $2 each and sells all of them for $3.50 each. What is the profit?
questions.explanation: Total cost is 50 × $2 = $100 and total income is 50 × $3.50 = $175, so the profit is $175 − $100 = $75. The tempting answer $175 is the total money taken in, not the profit, because it ignores what was spent buying the badges. Always subtract the total cost from the total income before reporting a profit.

questions.stem: Which calculation gives the percentage profit on an item, based on its cost price?
questions.explanation: Percentage profit compares the profit with the amount originally invested, so the cost price is the base of the comparison and the profit is divided by it before multiplying by 100. Dividing the profit by the selling price uses the wrong base and always gives a smaller figure than the true percentage profit. Ask yourself what amount the increase is being measured against — for profit it is what you paid.

questions.stem: Jo buys a second-hand bike for $450 and later sells it for $360. What is her percentage loss?
questions.explanation: The loss is $450 − $360 = $90, and as a percentage of the $450 cost price that is 90 ÷ 450 × 100 = 20%. Choosing 25% comes from dividing the $90 loss by the $360 selling price, which uses the wrong base. Percentage loss is always measured against what was originally paid.

questions.stem: A school fete stall models its profit with the rule: profit = 4n − 120, where n is the number of drinks sold. What does the 120 represent?
options: The fixed set-up costs the stall must cover
The profit made on each drink sold
The number of drinks the stall has to sell
The price in dollars charged for each drink
questions.explanation: In the rule, 4n is the money coming in from n drinks and the 120 is subtracted no matter how many are sold, so it must be a fixed cost such as hire or stock costs. Reading 120 as the number of drinks confuses a dollar amount with a count of items — n is the number of drinks, not 120. The coefficient of n tells you the per-item amount; the constant tells you the fixed amount.

questions.stem: A canteen spends $84 on ingredients and sells 60 muffins at $2.50 each. Which statement correctly interprets the result in context?
options: The canteen made a profit of $66
The canteen made a profit of $150
The canteen made a loss of $84
The canteen made a profit of $2.50
questions.explanation: Income is 60 × $2.50 = $150, and subtracting the $84 spent gives a profit of $66. Saying the profit is $150 mistakes total income for profit, since the ingredient cost has not been taken away. Interpreting in context means reporting the amount left over after costs, not the money collected.

questions.stem: Using the model profit = 4n − 120 for a drinks stall, how many drinks must be sold for the stall to break even (make neither a profit nor a loss)?
questions.explanation: Breaking even means profit = 0, so 4n = 120 and n = 30 drinks. Choosing 120 drinks reads the fixed cost as though it were a number of items, but 120 is measured in dollars. Set the profit expression equal to zero and solve for n whenever a question asks for break-even.

questions.stem: A shop buys a jacket for $40, marks it up by 60%, then sells it in a sale at 25% off the marked price. What is the shop's percentage profit on the cost price?
questions.explanation: The marked price is $40 × 1.6 = $64, and 25% off gives $64 × 0.75 = $48, so the profit is $8, which is 8 ÷ 40 × 100 = 20% of the cost price. Answering 35% comes from simply subtracting the two percentages, but the 25% discount applies to the larger marked price, not to the original $40. Percentage changes applied one after the other must be multiplied as decimals, not added or subtracted.

questions.stem: What is 0.4 as a fraction in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Four tenths cancels to two fifths. Leaving it as 4/10 is the right value but not the simplest form.

questions.stem: What is 3/8 as a decimal?
questions.explanation: Divide 3 by 8 to get 0.375, which terminates exactly. Any fraction whose denominator is a power of 2 or 5 terminates.

questions.stem: Calculate 2/3 + 1/4.
questions.explanation: Use a common denominator of 12: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12. Adding the tops and bottoms separately gives 3/7 and is the classic error.

questions.stem: Calculate 3/5 × 2/3.
questions.explanation: Multiply across to get 6/15, which cancels to 2/5. Multiplying fractions needs no common denominator, unlike adding.

questions.stem: Calculate 3/4 ÷ 1/2.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a fraction multiplies by its reciprocal: 3/4 × 2/1 = 3/2. Dividing by a number less than 1 always makes the result larger.

questions.stem: What is −7 + 12?
questions.explanation: Starting at −7 and moving 12 to the right lands on 5. A number line makes the direction of each move obvious.

questions.stem: What is −6 × −4?
questions.explanation: Two negatives multiplied give a positive. The same rule applies to division, which is worth learning as one fact.

questions.stem: What is −20 ÷ 5?
questions.explanation: One negative and one positive give a negative result. Counting how many negative signs are involved decides the sign every time.

questions.stem: Increase 60 by 25%.
questions.explanation: A quarter of 60 is 15, so the new value is 75. Giving 15 answers the increase rather than the total, which is a common misread.

questions.stem: What is 30% of 150?
questions.explanation: Ten percent is 15, so thirty percent is 45. Splitting into tens is faster and less error-prone than long multiplication.

questions.stem: A $80 jacket is reduced by 15%. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: The discount is $12, so the price is $68. Answering $12 gives the saving rather than what you pay.

questions.stem: What is the ratio 12:18 in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Divide both parts by 6. Reversing the order changes which quantity is which, so 3:2 describes a different situation.

questions.stem: Share $60 in the ratio 2:3.
questions.explanation: There are 5 parts in total, so each part is $12. Two parts are $24 and three are $36, and they add back to $60 as a check.

questions.stem: What is 5³?
questions.explanation: Cubing means multiplying by itself three times: 5 × 5 × 5. Multiplying the base by the index gives 15 and is the usual confusion.

questions.stem: What is the square root of 144?
questions.explanation: Twelve squared is 144. Halving the number gives 72, which confuses rooting with dividing by two.

questions.stem: Round 4.567 to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The third decimal is 7, so the second rounds up. Rounding to one place instead gives 4.6 and answers a different question.

questions.stem: Write 0.000045 in scientific notation.
questions.explanation: Move the point five places right to get 4.5, so the index is −5. Scientific notation needs exactly one non-zero digit before the point.

questions.stem: What is 2⁵ × 2³?
questions.explanation: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices. Multiplying the indices instead gives a far larger number.

questions.stem: Estimate 39 × 21 by rounding.
questions.explanation: Round to 40 × 20 = 800, which is close to the exact 819. Estimating first is how you catch an answer that is wildly wrong.

questions.stem: What is 7 − (−3)?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so this becomes 7 + 3. The two signs together reverse the direction of the move.

questions.stem: A recipe for 4 people uses 600 g of rice. How much for 7 people?
questions.explanation: Each person needs 150 g, so seven need 1050 g. Finding the amount for one first is the most reliable route through a proportion.

questions.stem: Which is larger, 0.6 or 3/5?
questions.explanation: Three fifths is exactly 0.6, so neither is larger. Converting to a common form is the only reliable way to compare.
